From this analysis, we can observe the number of charge-discharge events, estimate the total system load impacts for a defined suite of batteries, and quantify the estimated revenues from price arbitrage. The price profiles that exist in this study are numerous; for this analysis, we focus on two customer classes (residential and large C&I), for each of the three IOUs, in our two price forecast scenarios (low and high) and our three tariff design scenarios (full, medium, and mild), for a total of 36 price profiles. Figure 30 shows the number of times the battery completes a charge-discharge event18 across the year in response to each price profile. There is little difference in the number of events 18 Charge-discharge event refers to a time period of a battery charging, then discharging, before charging again. This is distinct from a battery “cycle”, which most commonly refers to a charge-discharge event in which the battery is completely charged and then completely drained. Events are discussed here to 47 across utilities, customer classes, and price forecast scenarios (low vs high); the main differences are across tariff design scenarios. Under the Full tariff, the battery has events twice every day (annual cycles 736-765), with about a month’s worth of days having three cycles. The Mild tariff results in the lowest number of cycles, as there are less opportunities for profitable price arbitrage due to the flatter price shape. Under the Mild tariff, the annual number of cycles ranges from 485-577, so approximately 1.5 cycles per day. The Medium tariff elicits 641-750 cycles per year, so an average of 1.75-2.05 cycles/day. The difference in BESS behavior varies across seasons, as shown in Figure 31. On all price designs, batteries tend to have two daily events during the winter. In the summer, a Full price profile will continue to drive two events per day, whereas on the Mild tariffs (and to a lesser extent, the medium tariffs), a majority of summer days only elicit one event in the afternoon/evening.
